title: Cueva del Chileno
subtitle: A high-Andean ritual bundle with direct chemical evidence for multiple psychoactive plants
summary: A concise archaeological site entry on Cueva del Chileno, a rock shelter in southwestern Bolivia where a 1,000-year-old ritual bundle preserves direct chemical evidence for coca, vilca or cebil, harmine-bearing plants, DMT-bearing plants, and possibly psilocin.
abstract: Cueva del Chileno is one of the strongest archaeological cases for pre-Columbian psychoactive plant use because the evidence is not based primarily on mythology, later texts, or speculative iconography. A ritual bundle recovered from the rock shelter included snuffing tablets, a snuffing tube, llama-bone spatulas, a textile band, dried plant fragments, and a pouch made from three fox snouts. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry detected cocaine, benzoylecgonine, bufotenine, harmine, dimethyltryptamine, and a possible psilocin signal, suggesting access to plants from distant ecological zones and a specialized ritual pharmacology in the late Tiwanaku or post-Tiwanaku south-central Andes.
editorial_note: Archaeological site description compiled from Miller et al. 2019 and institutional release materials from PNAS, Penn State, and UC Berkeley. The entry treats ayahuasca cautiously: harmine and DMT were detected together, but the exact ancient preparation cannot be reconstructed from residues alone.
citation: The Psychedelic History Archive. "Cueva del Chileno." Archaeological site entry, compiled from Miller et al. 2019 and cited archaeological reporting.
